segments.english: The king of Sodom went out to meet him, after his return from striking down Chedorlaomer and the kings who were with him, to the Valley of Shaveh, that is, the King's Valley.
segments.literal: and-went-out king-of Sodom to-meet-him after return-his from-striking [obj] Chedorlaomer and-[obj] the-kings who with-him to valley-of Shaveh it valley-of the-king

tokens.note: infinitive construct with ל and suffix
infinitive construct with suffix, temporal clause

phrases.english: The king of Sodom went out
and the kings who were with him

grammar: וַיֵּצֵא is a wayyiqtol: the narrative resumes after the battle report, with the king of Sodom as the new subject.
אַחֲרֵי שׁוּבוֹ and מֵהַכּוֹת are infinitives with suffix or preposition and form one time clause: 'after his returning from the striking of'.
The zinor on סְדֹם and the segol on לִקְרָאתוֹ set 'the king of Sodom ... to meet him' apart from the time clause; the etnaḥta on אִתּוֹ ends the first half.
הוּא עֵמֶק הַמֶּלֶךְ glosses the place name: 'that is, the King's Valley'.
segments.note: The English follows Rashi in taking עֵמֶק שָׁוֵה as the name of the place; Rashi and the Targum also give its sense as a cleared, level plain. The identity of 'the king' in הַמֶּלֶךְ is not stated; the name is kept as 'the King's Valley'.

commentary.summary: Rashi: 'so it is named', as Targum has it, 'a cleared plain': free of trees and every obstacle. He takes שָׁוֵה as a proper name that also describes the level ground.

Rashi: Targum's 'Beth Risa of the king', thirty reeds, reserved for the king to amuse himself there; the aggada says the nations agreed there to make Abraham ruler. The English keeps only the place name; both explanations are recorded.

apparatus: Onkelos renders עֵמֶק שָׁוֵה 'a cleared plain' and עֵמֶק הַמֶּלֶךְ 'the place Beth Risa of the king'.

segments.english: Now Melchizedek, king of Salem, brought out bread and wine. He was a priest of God Most High.
segments.literal: and-Malki-Tsedeq king-of Shalem brought-out bread and-wine and-he priest to-God Most-High

tokens.note: name read as 'my king is righteousness' or 'king of righteousness'
Ibn Ezra, Ramban and Radak: Salem is Jerusalem ('In Salem is his booth', Psalm 76:3)
adjective used as a divine epithet

phrases.literal: hifil of יצא, 'caused to go out'
'bread and-wine'; Rashi: food for men worn from war

grammar: The proper name has two parts joined by maqqef, מַלְכִּי־צֶדֶק. The pashta is written on the last letter of its word; because צֶדֶק is stressed on its first syllable, the accent is written a second time on the stressed syllable. The name can be read 'my king is Ṣedeq' or 'king of righteousness'.
הוֹצִיא is a hifil perfect, 'brought out'; the verb comes after its subject, so the clause is a new scene, not the next step in a chain of wayyiqtols.
וְהוּא כֹהֵן is a circumstantial clause giving his office: the pronoun opens the clause and the noun without article is the predicate.
אֵל עֶלְיוֹן: 'God Most High', the first appearance of the title.
segments.note: I give שָׁלֵם as Salem and record Jerusalem (Ibn Ezra, Ramban, Radak, citing Psalm 76:3). Rashi's 'Shem son of Noah' (so Radak) is recorded, not adopted, since it identifies the man and does not change the English. Rashi holds that the bread and wine were what one gives those weary from war (so also Radak and Sforno); Ibn Ezra does not comment on them. The Targum's 'ministered' (מְשַׁמֵּשׁ) for כֹהֵן, which Ibn Ezra adopts, is rendered 'was a priest'.

commentary.summary: Rashi: according to the aggada, Melchizedek is the name of Shem son of Noah (Nedarim 32). The English keeps the name only.

Rashi: so one treats those weary from battle, and he showed Abram he bore no grudge for killing his sons; the aggada has it hint at the offerings and libations. The English takes the plain sense of a meal for the weary.
Ibn Ezra: he was so called because he was king over a place of righteousness, though some say it is a personal name. The English keeps the name.
Ibn Ezra: 'Salem is Jerusalem', proved by 'In Salem is his booth' (Psalm 76:3). The English prints 'Salem' and records the identification here.

Ibn Ezra: as the Aramaic translator has it, כֹהֵן means one who ministers, as in וְכִהֲנוּ לִי; Melchizedek spoke properly in blessing Abram first for his zeal to rescue captives. The English says he was priest of God Most High.

apparatus: Onkelos: 'Melchizedek king of Jerusalem brought out bread and wine, and he ministered before God Most High'.

segments.english: He blessed him and said, "Blessed be Abram by God Most High, maker of heaven and earth."
segments.literal: and-blessed-him and-said blessed Abram to-God Most-High maker-of heavens and-earth

tokens.note: passive participle used as a blessing formula
לְ here 'by', 'to', 'for'; the blessing comes from God

phrases.literal: 'blessed Abram', passive participle in a wish
'to-God Most-High'; the לְ after a passive participle names the one from whom the blessing comes, 'by'
'maker-of heavens and-earth'; Rashi: קֹנֶה is like עֹשֶׂה, and by making them he made them his own

grammar: וַיְבָרְכֵהוּ is a piel wayyiqtol with the object suffix, followed by a second wayyiqtol that introduces the blessing itself.
בָּרוּךְ is a passive participle; there is no verb 'be', so the wish is a verbless clause 'blessed Abram to God Most High'.
קֹנֵה is a construct participle of קנה; it can mean 'buyer', 'owner', or 'maker', the last attested for the root in Deuteronomy 32:6 and Psalm 139:13.
The accents divide the blessing: the zaqef on עֶלְיוֹן separates the blessing from the title 'maker of heaven and earth'.
segments.note: קֹנֵה is read 'maker' with Rashi (קֹנֶה like עֹשֶׂה, and by making them he acquired them as his own) and Radak (not one who buys from another, but one who makes or brings into being). Ramban holds the main sense is ownership, 'whose possession they are', and says Onkelos meant this by דִּקִנְיָנֵיהּ; that reading is recorded in the apparatus. בָּרוּךְ is a Qal passive participle.

commentary.summary: Rashi: קֹנֵה is like עֹשֵׂה (Psalm 134), and by making heaven and earth he acquired them to be his. The English takes 'maker' and records 'acquirer' here.

apparatus: Onkelos has 'to God Most High whose possession is heaven and earth' (דִּקִנְיָנֵיהּ); Radak says 'make or provide'; Sforno 'heaven and earth are a possession for him'.

segments.english: And blessed be God Most High, who has delivered your enemies into your hand. And Abram gave him a tenth of everything.
segments.literal: and-blessed God Most-High who delivered your-foes in-your-hand and-gave to-him tenth from-all

tokens.note: passive participle in a blessing formula
wayyiqtol; Rashi: the subject is Abram

phrases.english: And blessed be God Most High

phrases.literal: 'and-gave to-him', the subject Abram supplied after Rashi

grammar: מִגֵּן is a piel perfect, 'delivered up', as Rashi (הִסְגִּיר, Hosea 11:8) and Ibn Ezra (like נָתַן, Proverbs 4:9) say, not 'shielded'. The lexicon files it under the root גנן, which gives מָגֵן 'shield'; Ibn Ezra holds that the מ is a root letter.
צָרֶיךָ is a plural construct (צָרֵי) with the suffix ךָ: 'your adversaries'.
The pashta on בָּרוּךְ and the zaqef on עֶלְיוֹן divide the blessing from its relative clause.
וַיִּתֶּן־לוֹ has no stated subject; the reader must decide who gives to whom, and Rashi says Abram gave.
segments.note: Rashi and Ibn Ezra agree that מִגֵּן means 'handed over', like נָתַן, and the English follows them rather than 'shielded'. The subject of וַיִּתֶּן is Abram (Rashi, Ibn Ezra); the other reading, that Melchizedek gave Abram a tithe, is a real alternative that the Hebrew does not exclude, and I do not adopt it.

commentary.summary: Rashi: אֲשֶׁר מִגֵּן means 'who handed over', like אֲמַגֶּנְךָ יִשְׂרָאֵל (Hosea 11).
Rashi: the giver is Abraham. The English names Abram.
Rashi: the tithe was from all that Abram had, because Melchizedek was a priest. The English says 'of everything'.

Ibn Ezra: מִגֵּן is like נָתַן, as in 'a crown of glory she shall deliver you' (Proverbs 4:9); the מ is a root letter; Abram took out the tithe in honor of God and found no one fitter than Melchizedek.

segments.english: The king of Sodom said to Abram, "Give me the people, and take the goods for yourself."
segments.literal: and-said king-of Sodom to Abram give to-me the-person and-the-goods take for-you

tokens.note: collective singular; Rashi: the persons, the bodies
reflexive dative, 'for yourself'; the pausal form of לְךָ at the silluq, masculine singular. The pack parses it feminine.

phrases.literal: 'give to-me the-nefesh'; Rashi: the persons themselves

phrases.english: and take the goods for yourself
phrases.literal: 'and-the-goods take for-you': the verb stands after its object

grammar: נֶפֶשׁ with the article is a collective singular, 'the persons'; the word does not mean 'soul' here but the living captives.
The two imperatives תֶּן and קַח are set against each other: the king asks for the people and offers the goods.
הָרְכֻשׁ is placed before its verb for contrast with הַנֶּפֶשׁ.
לָךְ is the pausal form of לְךָ 'to you' (masculine singular): at the silluq the suffix is written ךְ with qamets under the ל. The same form returns at the etnaḥta in 14:23.
segments.note: The pack parses the suffix of לָךְ as feminine; the form is the pausal ךְ spelling, and the sense is addressed to Abram. I keep the pack's data and note it here. 'The people' follows Rashi's 'the bodies alone'.

commentary.summary: Rashi: 'from my captives whom you rescued, return to me the bodies alone'. The English takes נֶפֶשׁ as the captured persons.

segments.english: Abram said to the king of Sodom, "I raise my hand in oath to the LORD, God Most High, maker of heaven and earth:
segments.literal: and-said Abram to king-of Sodom I-raise my-hand to YHWH God Most-High maker-of heavens and-earth

tokens.note: hifil perfect; the perfect of a performative oath, 'I hereby raise'

phrases.english: I raise my hand in oath
phrases.literal: 'I-raise my-hand'; Rashi, Ibn Ezra: an oath

grammar: הֲרִמֹתִי is a hifil perfect with a performative sense: the act of raising the hand is the oath, as Rashi's parallel with 'I have sworn' (22:16) shows.
The name יְהוָה is added to Melchizedek's title: Abram says 'the LORD, God Most High', identifying the two.
The oath continues through verse 24 and does not end at the silluq.
The qadma on הֲרִמֹתִי and the mahpakh on יָדִי hold the oath formula together.
segments.note: The English renders the gesture and gives its sense, an oath, with Rashi and Ibn Ezra, who agree. Abram adds the divine name יְהוָה to the title used by Melchizedek (Ibn Ezra: 'I swore by the name by which this priest blessed me').

commentary.summary: Rashi: the phrase is the language of an oath: 'I raise my hand to God Most High', like 'I have sworn by myself' (22:16) and 'I give you the field' (23:13). The English says 'in oath'.
Ibn Ezra: an oath, as in 'I raise my hand to heaven' (Deuteronomy 32:40).
Ibn Ezra: the sense of אֵל עֶלְיוֹן is that I swore by the name by which this priest blessed me. The English keeps the title.

apparatus: 14:22.6: MAM writes הֲרִמֹתִי (defective); WLC writes הֲרִימֹתִי (plene), the spelling of Ibn Ezra's and Ramban's lemmas. The sense is the same.

segments.english: I will not take so much as a thread or a sandal strap, nor anything that is yours, so that you cannot say, 'I made Abram rich.'
segments.literal: if from-thread and-up-to strap-of sandal and-if I-take from-all who to-you and-not you-say I I-enriched [obj] Abram

tokens.note: pausal form of לְךָ at the etnaḥta, masculine singular; the pack parses it feminine
וְלֹא; the clause gives the reason of the refusal

phrases.english: I will not take so much as a thread or a sandal strap
phrases.literal: 'if from-thread and-up-to strap-of sandal'; an oath, 'if I take...' meaning 'I will not'

grammar: The oath formula אִם ... אִם takes a negative sense: 'if I take ... may I be ...', that is 'I will not take'; the penalty is left unsaid.
מִחוּט וְעַד שְׂרוֹךְ־נַעַל is an idiom for 'the smallest thing', from a thread to a shoe strap.
הֶעֱשַׁרְתִּי is the hifil of עָשַׁר, the causative of the Qal 'be rich': 'I made rich'. The pronoun אֲנִי, not needed with a finite verb, stresses the claim: 'I, I made'.
The etnaḥta on לָךְ ends the oath, and וְלֹא תֹאמַר starts the clause giving the purpose.
segments.note: אִם is the elliptical oath, 'not' (so Rashi's 'I will keep back for myself nothing from the captives'). Rashi reads the second clause as 'if you offer me a reward from your treasury, I will not take it' and the third as God's promise to enrich Abram (12:2), which is the reason; both bear on the sense but not on the wording of the English.

commentary.summary: Rashi: 'I will keep for myself nothing of the captives', the sense of אִם as an oath.
Rashi: if you say to give me wages from your treasury, I will not take them. The English says 'nor anything that is yours'.
Rashi: Abram refuses because the Holy One had promised to make him rich, as it says 'and I will bless you' (12:2). The English is consistent; the reason is not stated in the text.
Ibn Ezra: חוּט is the thread from which every garment is sewn.
Ibn Ezra: שְׂרוֹךְ is the leather that binds the sandal.

segments.english: Not for me, only what my servants have eaten, and the share of the men who went with me: Aner, Eshcol and Mamre. They may take their share."
segments.literal: apart-from-me only what ate the-lads and-share-of the-men who went with-me Aner Eshcol and-Mamre they let-them-take share-their

tokens.note: perfect plural, 'went'. The pack lists no sense for the plain Qal 'go'; Qal II.2 'live, walk' is a way of life, not movement, so no sense is given.

phrases.english: only what my servants have eaten
phrases.literal: 'only what ate the-lads'; Rashi and Ibn Ezra: Abram's own servants

phrases.english: and the share of the men

phrases.literal: three men without conjunction until the last

grammar: בִּלְעָדַי is a preposition with suffix meaning 'apart from me'; it opens the verse without a verb, as a stand-alone refusal.
רַק limits what follows: only the food eaten and the allies' portion are excepted from the oath.

The names עָנֵר אֶשְׁכֹּל וּמַמְרֵא stand in apposition to הָאֲנָשִׁים; the zaqef on וּמַמְרֵא closes the list, and the tipḥa on הֵם and the silluq end the closing clause 'they shall take their share'.
יִקְחוּ is jussive in sense: 'let them take'; הֵם adds emphasis, 'let them, for their part'.
segments.note: Rashi and Ibn Ezra agree that הַנְּעָרִים are Abram's servants, so the English says 'my servants' (literally 'the lads'). Rashi adds that though the servants fought, Aner and his companions stayed with the baggage, yet they take a share (David learned from this).

commentary.summary: Rashi: הַנְּעָרִים are my servants who went with me; though they fought and Aner, Eshcol and Mamre stayed with the baggage, they take their share, and David learned from it. The English says 'my servants'.
Ibn Ezra: 'what the young men have eaten' means what his servants ate.
